Ledgerly uses Django with Django REST Framework (DRF). The team built it as a monolith backend since they're a small team with one deploy target, paired with a React frontend that communicates with the DRF API.

Based on the transcripts from earlier sessions, money amounts are stored as **cents in bigint columns** (e.g., `total_cents` and `unit_cents`). This approach avoids floating-point precision issues when handling financial calculations.

Based on session s14-mollie, **Mollie** is the payment provider for new customers as of June 17, 2026. The team switched from Stripe to Mollie because Mollie's flat fee per transaction is more cost-effective for invoices above 100 euros.

Stripe charged a percentage on SEPA Direct Debit payments, while Mollie charges a flat fee per transaction, which is much cheaper for invoices above 100 euros. This cost savings was the key driver for switching payment providers.

Invoice numbers follow the format `LDG-YYYY-NNNNN` (e.g., `LDG-2026-00042`), with the counter resetting every January. Numbers must be gapless to comply with German tax rules (GoBD), so they are allocated within the same transaction that finalizes the invoice.

Invoice numbers must have no gaps because German tax rules (GoBD) do not allow holes in the sequence. The team allocates invoice numbers inside the same transaction that finalizes the invoice to ensure compliance.

Puppeteer kept crashing because headless Chrome required more than the 512 MB memory available in the container. WeasyPrint was chosen as an alternative since it renders HTML templates without needing a browser.
Tests run against a real Postgres database started with testcontainers. The team moved away from SQLite because it was hiding bugs with bigint and row locking.

The server was running in UTC and the invoice date was being derived from a UTC timestamp, causing invoices finalized shortly after midnight to be dated one day too early. The fix was to derive the `issued_on` date from the Europe/Berlin local date instead and add a test for 00:30 local time.

The team chose Postmark over SendGrid because during testing, SendGrid emails landed in spam at GMX and web.de, which are the primary email providers used by most of Ledgerly's German customers. Postmark had better deliverability to those German mail providers.
Users log in to Ledgerly with magic links sent by email; the system does not store passwords. The links expire after 15 minutes and can only be used once.
No, the team no longer uses Unleash. In session s13-flags-removed (June 2026), they decided Unleash was overkill and replaced all feature flags with environment variables read at startup.

The team added an idempotency key on the payment intent id with a unique constraint on the payments table, so retried webhooks from Stripe would be treated as a no-op instead of creating duplicate payment records. This ensured that when Stripe retried the webhook after a timeout, the second attempt would hit the unique constraint and not create a duplicate invoice.
The Pro plan costs 29 euros per month. It adds automatic dunning and custom invoice templates compared to the Starter plan (which costs 9 euros per month).
Dunning reminders are sent 7, 14, and 30 days after the invoice due date. The first two are friendly reminders without a fee, while the third reminder (at 30 days) adds a late fee of 5 euros.
The public API rate limit is 60 requests per minute per API key. Requests exceeding this limit receive a 429 response with a Retry-After header.

Database backups are kept for 30 days—the team performs nightly pg_dump exports to Hetzner's S3-compatible object storage with 30-day retention, and they test a restore on the first Monday of every month.
Ledgerly uses **i18next** for translations. The team wraps UI strings with i18next instead of hardcoding German text, supporting German as the primary language with English to follow.

Ledgerly uses **Django** as the backend framework with Django REST Framework. The team decided to start as a single Django monolith rather than using microservices since there are only two developers.
The team stores all money as integer cents in bigint columns, never as floats or Decimal. Rounding happens once when rendering the invoice.

The team switched to Mollie in June 2026 as the payment provider for new customers because Mollie charges a flat fee per transaction, which is cheaper than Stripe's percentage-based fees for SEPA Direct Debit on invoices above 100 euros. Existing Stripe customers are being migrated by end of July 2026.
